paragraphs: The social compact gave the body politic existence and life. Legislation must now give it movement and will, because the original act that formed and united the body does not settle at all what the body should do to preserve itself.

What is good and orderly is so by the nature of things, whatever human agreements say. All justice comes from God, its only source. If we knew how to receive such a high inspiration, we would need no government and no laws. There is, no doubt, a universal justice that springs from reason alone. But for us to accept it, it has to work both ways. Speaking in human terms, the laws of justice have no force among men when nature supplies no sanctions: they only help the wicked and hurt the just, if the just man obeys them toward everyone while nobody obeys them toward him. So conventions and laws are needed to tie rights to duties and to bring justice to its object. In the state of nature, where everything is common, I owe nothing to anyone I have promised nothing; I recognize as belonging to others only what is of no use to me. In the state of society the law fixes all rights, and things are different.

But what, after all, is a law? So long as we only attach purely metaphysical ideas to the word, we will keep arguing without understanding one another. And even once we have defined a law of nature, we will be no closer to defining a law of the State.

I have already said that no general will can be directed at a particular object. That object must lie either inside the State or outside it. If it lies outside, a will that is foreign to the State is not general with respect to it. If it lies inside, it is part of the State, and then a relation arises between whole and part that makes them two separate beings: the part is one, and the whole minus that part is the other. But the whole minus a part is not the whole. As long as this relation lasts there is no whole, only two unequal parts, and so the will of one is no longer in any respect general toward the other.

But when the whole people makes decrees for the whole people, it considers only itself. If any relation arises, it is between two aspects of one entire object, and the whole is not divided. Then the subject of the decree is general, just as the will that decrees it is general. This act is what I call a law.

When I say that the object of laws is always general, I mean that a law looks at subjects _en masse_ and at actions in the abstract, never at a particular person or a particular action. So a law can decree that there will be privileges, but it cannot grant them to anyone by name. It can create several classes of citizens and even set the qualifications for each class, but it cannot say which persons belong to them. It can establish a monarchical government with hereditary succession, but it cannot pick a king or name a royal family. In short, any function that has a particular object lies outside the legislative power.

From this view it follows at once that nobody needs to ask whose business it is to make laws, since they are acts of the general will; or whether the prince is above the law, since he is a member of the State; or whether the law can be unjust, since no one is unjust to himself; or how we can be free and yet subject to the laws, since they only record our own wills.

We see further that the law joins a universal will to a universal object. So whatever a man, whoever he is, commands on his own account cannot be a law. Even what the Sovereign commands about a particular matter comes no closer to being a law: it is a decree, an act not of sovereignty but of magistracy.

I therefore call every State that is governed by laws a ‘Republic,’ whatever its form of administration may be. Only there does the public interest govern and the _res publica_ count as a _reality_. Every legitimate government is republican;[1] I will explain later what government is.

Laws are, strictly speaking, nothing but the conditions of civil association. The people who are subject to the laws ought to be their authors, and only those who join together to form the society should set its conditions. But how are they to set them? By common agreement, on a sudden inspiration? Does the body politic have an organ to declare its will? Who will give it the foresight to draft its acts and announce them in advance? Or how will it announce them when the need arises? How can a blind multitude, which often does not know what it wants because it rarely knows what is good for it, carry out by itself an undertaking as great and difficult as a system of legislation? On its own, the people always wills the good, but on its own it does not always see it. The general will is always right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened. The people must be made to see things as they are, and sometimes as they ought to appear to it. It must be shown the good road it is searching for, shielded from the seductions of individual wills, taught to see times and places as a series, and made to weigh the pull of present, visible advantages against the danger of distant, hidden evils. Individuals see the good and reject it; the public wills the good and does not see it. Both need guidance. The first must be forced to bring their wills into line with their reason; the second must be taught to know what it wills. When that is done, public enlightenment unites understanding and will in the social body, so that the parts work together exactly and the whole is raised to its greatest strength. This is what makes a legislator necessary.
